name: Epristeride

lead: Epristeride is an oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that people in hair-loss communities discuss as a finasteride-like way to hold on to scalp hair. It is sold in China for enlarged prostate.

It blocks the type 2 form of the enzyme that turns testosterone into DHT, the hormone linked to follicle miniaturisation and pattern hair loss. Less DHT means less thinning over time. Hair loss and acne were explored as uses during development but were never approved, and no published hair-loss trial results turned up.

paras: People who use it treat it as an alternative to finasteride, taken by mouth as a daily tablet, usually alongside other hair-loss measures. Hair-loss drugs of this type are generally kept up long term, with results judged over many months.
Safety information is sparse. As a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor it is prescription-only where it is marketed, and it is not sold in the US, UK or Japan.

angle.text: Epristeride lowers DHT, the hormone that shrinks scalp follicles, so the goal is slower thinning and more hair kept. Hair-loss forum users discuss it as a finasteride-like option. It is marketed in China for prostate enlargement, and its hair use was explored but never approved.

lead: Epristeride is an oral steroidal 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that lowers conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). It is marketed in China for benign prostatic hyperplasia under brand names including Aipuliete and Chuanliu [1].

It was also investigated for male pattern hair loss and acne, but those uses were never approved, according to Wikipedia [1]. It is therefore of interest to hair-loss communities as a finasteride-like compound, although the sources reviewed contain no hair-loss trial results.
Laboratory work describes it as a selective inhibitor of the type 2 isoform of the enzyme [2].

paras: Epristeride is used in China for benign prostatic hyperplasia [1]. Wikipedia states that it was studied for androgenic alopecia and acne without receiving approval for either [1].

It inhibits the type 2 isoform of 5-alpha-reductase through an uncompetitive mechanism, forming a complex with the enzyme, testosterone and NADPH [1][2]. Comparative tissue work examined its sensitivity alongside finasteride [3]. Wikipedia reports that it lowers circulating DHT by only about 25 to 54% despite high in-vitro potency [1].
Wikipedia gives oral bioavailability of about 93% and an elimination half-life of about 26 hours [1].

No studies found for hair loss. The sources reviewed contain laboratory and cell-culture research on its enzyme inhibition and effects on prostate cells [2][3][4], and Wikipedia mentions that it reached phase III trials for BPH, androgenic alopecia and acne in the US, UK and Japan without being marketed there [1].

SmithKline Beecham developed epristeride in the 1990s for BPH, androgenic alopecia and acne. It was not marketed in the US, UK or Japan. Ono Pharmaceutical developed and introduced it for BPH in China in 2000 [1].

timeline.event: Laboratory study describes epristeride as a selective inhibitor of human 5-alpha-reductase type 2 [2].
